JSON: Name: e_satisfaction_e_trust_repurchase_students_bd Title: Structural equation modeling and simultaneous-equation analysis of e-satisfaction, e-trust, and online repurchase intention among university students in a developing country Short Hypothesis: An increase in e-customer satisfaction causes a statistically significant increase in online repurchase intention among university students. Related Work: Prior work models online repurchase and purchase intention using theory-driven frameworks (TRA, TPB, TAM/UTAUT) and estimation via SEM or PLS-SEM. Typical studies treat predictors (website design, price fairness, delivery service, e-service quality, security, e-WOM) as exogenous inputs and e-satisfaction and e-trust as mediators or direct predictors of repurchase intention. Common limitations are (1) reliance on single-theory formulations rather than integrated models, (2) heavy dependence on cross-sectional self-report surveys from developed-market samples, (3) limited attention to endogeneity or simultaneity among satisfaction, trust, and intention, (4) sparse robustness checks against alternative estimators, (5) inconsistent treatment of mediators and moderators (especially prior online experience), and (6) frequent omission of explicit tests for common-method variance and measurement/model misspecification. Abstract: This research addresses the determinants of online repurchase intention among university students in a developing-country context by integrating e-customer satisfaction and e-trust into a unified structural model and corroborating results with a simultaneous-equation estimator. Using an integrated theoretical frame, the study estimates direct and indirect effects of website design, price fairness, delivery service, e-service quality, security/privacy, and electronic word-of-mouth on repurchase intention, and tests prior online experience as a moderator. The main methodological contribution is a two-pronged estimation strategy: confirmatory structural equation modeling for measurement validity and path inference, and two-stage least-squares simultaneous-equation estimation to evaluate robustness to endogeneity and simultaneity among mediators. Expected outcomes include quantified path coefficients, validated mediation and moderation paths, and robustness diagnostics that distinguish genuine causal associations from artifacts of cross-sectional survey data. Results will offer empirically grounded priorities for interventions to increase repeat online purchases among student populations and provide a replicable pipeline for future cross-cultural studies. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = N=415 completed responses from university students in the southern region of Bangladesh (structured questionnaire with multi-item Likert scales for all constructs). Optional external replication datasets: (a) N>=400 students from a different region in Bangladesh, (b) N>=400 students from a comparable developing country. Baselines: (1) measurement-only CFA; (2) conventional SEM (maximum likelihood) estimating all direct and mediated paths; (3) PLS-SEM variant; (4) OLS regressions on aggregated indices; (5) simultaneous-equation estimation using two-stage least squares (2SLS). Preprocessing: remove incomplete records, inspect for straight-lining, impute at item level with item median if <5% missing, compute construct scores and check skewness/kurtosis. Evaluation metrics: model fit (χ2/df, CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR), explanatory power (R2 for endogenous variables), standardized path coefficients with robust SE and p-values, bootstrapped indirect effects (5,000 resamples) with 95% CIs, VIF for multicollinearity, Durbin-Watson and endogeneity tests (Hausman test) for potentially endogenous mediators, Harman’s single-factor and a common-method latent factor test for CMV. Experimental steps: (A) validate measurement model via CFA; (B) estimate structural SEM and record path coefficients, R2, and fit; (C) test mediation using bootstrapped indirect effects; (D) test moderation by prior online experience via multi-group SEM and interaction terms; (E) estimate simultaneous-equation system (2SLS) where e-satisfaction and e-trust are endogenous, use external instruments where available (e.g., exogenous variation in delivery service or regional internet quality); (F) compare coefficients and significance between SEM and 2SLS (report differences and overidentification statistics); (G) ablation studies: remove (i) e-WOM, (ii) security, (iii) customer service quality and re-estimate models to assess changes in R2 and focal coefficients; (H) subgroup analyses: urban vs rural, age bands, and education level; (I) report robustness tables that include standardized coefficients, SEs, p-values, bootstrapped CIs, fit indices, VIFs, Durbin-Watson, and Hausman/overidentification test results. Significance thresholds: two-sided p<0.05 primary, p<0.01 strong. Reproducibility: provide code for CFA/SEM (e.g., lavaan/AMOS) and 2SLS estimations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample and generalization: university-student sample from one region limits external validity to other age groups, regions, product categories, or countries. Cross-sectional design: temporal ordering is not observed, constraining causal inference despite 2SLS; reverse causality may remain. Measurement bias: self-reported Likert items incur social desirability and recall bias; common-method variance may inflate correlations. Endogeneity and instrument quality: valid external instruments for e-satisfaction and e-trust may be unavailable or weak, reducing 2SLS reliability. Model misspecification: omitted variables (e.g., socioeconomic status, device type, product category) can bias estimates. Statistical power: subgroup and multi-group tests require larger samples; current N=415 may be underpowered for complex multi-group moderation. Computational/estimation limits: nonnormal indicators, small sample, or multicollinearity can destabilize SEM or 2SLS estimates. Cultural specificity: constructs (e.g., perceived price fairness, e-WOM) may have different meanings across cultures, limiting transferability of parameter estimates.
